etymology: Hebrew Parah, perhaps “heifer” or “the place of the cow,” a town in the allotment of Benjamin.
biblical_def: Parah was a small town in the inheritance of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the list of its cities between Avim and Ophrah (Jos 18:23). It is one of the many places of which Scripture records the name and little else, a single dot upon the map of the apportioned land. The cities of Benjamin were numbered according to their families, beginning with Jericho and Beth-hoglah and the valley of Keziz (Jos 18:21), and among them Parah took its appointed place. The dictionary does not multiply conjectures about so obscure a town; it honours instead the great doctrine the bare name teaches. Every city of the inheritance was assigned by lot, and the lot was cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof was of the LORD (Pro 16:33). The portion of Benjamin, like the portion of every tribe, was no accident of geography or of war, but the gift of God, who is Himself the portion of His people’s inheritance and of their cup, and who maintains their lot (Psa 16:5). Parah stands for the truth that the smallest and least-remembered place in the heritage of the saints is held and measured by the faithful hand of God.
webster_summary: A small town in the allotment of Benjamin, named among the cities of the tribe.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the providence of God over the casting of the lot. The lot was thrown into the lap, but its whole disposing was of the LORD; nothing in the apportioning of Benjamin was left to chance. So the believer learns that the bounds of his own portion, however small, are measured and maintained by the same faithful God, and that no part of his heritage falls outside the care of Him who is Himself his portion and his cup.

etymology: Hebrew Yebus, the older name of Jerusalem, the city of the Jebusites, “the trodden place” or “threshing-floor.”
biblical_def: Jebus was the ancient name of the city that became Jerusalem, called after the Jebusites who held its stronghold from the days of the conquest. The Scripture plainly identifies the two, saying that David and all Israel went to Jerusalem, which is Jebus, where the Jebusites were, the inhabitants of the land (1Ch 11:4; and Jdg 19:10). For long years the city stood unconquered in the very midst of the inheritance, for the children of Judah could not drive out the Jebusites, who dwelt with them at Jerusalem unto that day (Jos 15:63). It was a fortress of pride, thought impregnable, until David took the strong hold of Zion, the same which became the city of David (2Sa 5:7). The dictionary marks Jebus as the heathen stronghold transformed by conquest into the city of God. What had been the seat of the Jebusite and his idols became the place of the throne of David, the resting-place of the ark, and the site of the temple where the LORD set His name. So the gospel takes the strongholds of man’s rebellion and, by the conquest of the true Son of David, makes of them the dwelling-place of God; and the city long held against Him becomes at last the city of the great King.

etymology: Hebrew Pisgah, “the cleft” or “the ridge,” the height of the mountain of Nebo from which Moses viewed the promised land.
biblical_def: Pisgah was the height, or the ridge, of the mountain of Nebo in the land of Moab, over against Jericho. From its top the LORD shewed Moses all the land of promise, from Gilead unto Dan, and unto the utmost sea (Deu 34:1). It was a place of both vision and sorrow. Moses was bidden to get up into the top of Pisgah and lift up his eyes westward and northward and southward and eastward, and behold the land with his eyes, for he should not go over Jordan (Deu 3:27). And the LORD said, This is the land which I sware unto Abraham, unto Isaac, and unto Jacob; I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither (Deu 34:4). The dictionary marks Pisgah as the mount of seeing but not entering. The law, in the person of its great minister, could bring Israel to the very border of the inheritance and show it from afar, but could not carry the people in; that was reserved for Joshua, whose name is the name of Jesus. So Pisgah teaches that the saints die in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and embraced them (Heb 11:13), assured that what the law shows from the height, Christ bestows in full.

etymology: Hebrew En-Dor, “spring of Dor” or “fountain of habitation,” a town of Manasseh, infamous as the dwelling of the woman with a familiar spirit.
biblical_def: En-dor was a town belonging to the half-tribe of Manasseh within the borders of Issachar and Asher, named among the towns Manasseh held but did not fully possess (Jos 17:11). It is remembered above all for the darkest night of Saul’s reign. When the king, forsaken of God and answered neither by dreams nor by Urim nor by prophets, sought a woman that had a familiar spirit, his servants told him there was such a woman at Endor (1Sa 28:7). Thither Saul went by night in disguise, to enquire of the dead what the living God would not tell him. The Chronicler sets down the verdict of heaven: Saul died for his transgression, and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it, and enquired not of the LORD (1Ch 10:13). The dictionary marks En-dor as the place of forbidden enquiry, where apostasy reached its end in necromancy. The prophet Isaiah pressed the same reproof upon all generations: when men bid you seek unto them that have familiar spirits, that peep and mutter, should not a people seek unto their God? For the living to the dead? (Isa 8:19). En-dor stands as the warning that the soul which turns from God turns at last to the pit, and finds there no light at all.
webster_summary: A town of Manasseh where the woman with a familiar spirit dwelt, the scene of Saul’s last apostasy.

etymology: Hebrew Yible’am, perhaps “he consumes the people,” a town of Manasseh in the plain of Jezreel.
biblical_def: Ibleam was a town belonging to the half-tribe of Manasseh, set among the cities of the plain with Beth-shean, Taanach, and Megiddo (Jos 17:11). Like its neighbours, it was a town Manasseh could not, or would not, possess, for neither did Manasseh drive out the inhabitants of Ibleam and her towns, but the Canaanites would dwell in that land (Jdg 1:27). Thus Ibleam belongs to the sad register of the unfinished conquest, the cities suffered to remain in the heart of the inheritance against the plain command of God, who had said, Ye shall make no league with the inhabitants of this land; ye shall throw down their altars (Jdg 2:2). In the days of the kings the town saw a violent end, for it was by the going up to Gur, which is by Ibleam, that Jehu’s men smote Ahaziah king of Judah in his chariot, and he fled to Megiddo and died there (2Ki 9:27). The dictionary marks Ibleam as a town of compromise and of judgment. What Israel failed to cleanse remained a snare, and the plains they would not purge of idolatry became in time the very fields of blood where kings fell under the avenging hand of God.
webster_summary: A town of Manasseh in the plain of Jezreel, left unconquered and later a scene of royal bloodshed.

corruption_paragraphs: Ibleam has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as a name in the record of Manasseh’s failure and Ahaziah’s fall. The dictionary records the town that the reader may mark how a spared idolatry returned in time as a field of blood.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the danger of a league with what God commanded to be destroyed. Manasseh suffered the Canaanite to dwell at Ibleam against the voice of the LORD, and the unpurged plain became at last the place where a king was struck down. So the believer is warned that the idols he will not cast out abide to his hurt, and the compromise spared in mercy becomes in time a snare and a sorrow.

etymology: Hebrew Megiddo, perhaps “place of troops” or “rendezvous,” a fortress city commanding the great plain of Esdraelon.
biblical_def: Megiddo was a fortress city of the half-tribe of Manasseh, set where the pass opens upon the great plain of Esdraelon, the highway of armies between Egypt and the north. It was a town Manasseh held but did not cleanse of its Canaanites (Jos 17:11). Its plain was a famous field of battle from the days of the judges, when the kings of Canaan fought in Taanach by the waters of Megiddo (Jdg 5:19). There Josiah, the last good king of Judah, would not turn from his rash war against Pharaoh-nechoh, but came to fight in the valley of Megiddo, and was slain (2Ki 23:29; 2Ch 35:22), so that the plain became the place of Judah’s deepest mourning. From this storied field of slaughter the Spirit took a name for the last great conflict of the age, gathering the kings of the earth to a place called in the Hebrew tongue Armageddon, the hill of Megiddo (Rev 16:16). The dictionary marks Megiddo as the battlefield of the ages. Where the chariots of the heathen and the body of a godly king alike went down, the prophetic word sets the figure of the final overthrow of all the powers gathered against the Lord and against His Christ.
webster_summary: A fortress city on the plain of Esdraelon, a famous field of battle and the root of the name Armageddon.

The believer reads in this ancient battlefield the pledge that every power arrayed against God shall fall at last upon the field of His appointing.

etymology: Hebrew Adummim, “the red places” or “places of blood,” a steep ascent on the road between Jericho and Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Adummim, “the going up to Adummim,” was a steep and rocky ascent on the boundary between Judah and Benjamin, on the lonely road that climbs from Jericho up to Jerusalem (Jos 15:7; Jos 18:17). Its name, “the red,” was anciently traced to the colour of its rocks, but also to the blood shed by the robbers who haunted that dangerous pass. The dictionary marks the place because the Lord Jesus set His most famous parable upon this very road, telling of a certain man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves, which stripped him and wounded him, and departed, leaving him half dead (Luk 10:30). Priest and Levite passed by on the other side; but a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion on him (Luk 10:33). So the bloody ascent of Adummim became the scene of the great picture of mercy. The man fallen among thieves is fallen Adam, stripped and half dead in sin; the priest and Levite are the law that cannot save; and the despised Samaritan who binds his wounds is Christ, who alone draws near to the helpless and pays the whole price of their healing. The road of blood is made the highway of grace.
webster_summary: A steep ascent between Jericho and Jerusalem, the road of the parable of the good Samaritan.

etymology: Hebrew En-Rogel, “the fuller’s fountain” or “spring of the spy,” a spring on the boundary of Judah and Benjamin near Jerusalem.
biblical_def: En-rogel was a spring at the meeting of the valleys below Jerusalem, marking the boundary between Judah and Benjamin (Jos 15:7; Jos 18:16). In the days of Absalom’s revolt, Jonathan and Ahimaaz stayed at En-rogel, that they might not be seen entering the city, and a maidservant carried David’s tidings to them there (2Sa 17:17). But the spring is chiefly remembered for the feast of Adonijah. When David was old, Adonijah the son of Haggith exalted himself, saying, I will be king, and prepared him chariots and horsemen and fifty men to run before him (1Ki 1:5). He slew sheep and oxen and fat cattle by the stone of Zoheleth, which is by En-rogel, and called all the king’s sons and the men of Judah to his usurping feast (1Ki 1:9). Yet even as Adonijah feasted, the LORD’s chosen, Solomon, was anointed at Gihon by the king’s command, and the cry of the people undid the rebel’s banquet. The dictionary marks En-rogel as the spring of vain self-exaltation. Adonijah set himself up and gathered his guests, but he had not the word of the LORD nor the appointment of the king; and the man who exalts himself against the purpose of God prepares only the feast of his own undoing.
webster_summary: A spring near Jerusalem where Adonijah held the usurping feast that came to nothing.

Adonijah exalted himself, gathered his guests, and feasted by En-rogel, but he had neither the word of the LORD nor the appointment of the king, and his banquet was scattered when Solomon was anointed. So every man who lifts himself up against the counsel of heaven prepares only the feast of his own undoing; for whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased.

etymology: Hebrew Mitspeh, “watchtower” or “place of outlook,” a town of Benjamin, the great gathering-place of Israel in the days of Samuel.
biblical_def: Mizpeh of Benjamin was a high place of outlook north of Jerusalem, and it became one of the chief gathering-places of Israel for assembly and for prayer. Thither all the children of Israel came out as one man, from Dan even to Beersheba, to seek the LORD against the great wickedness of Gibeah (Jdg 20:1). And there Samuel called the nation to repentance, saying, Gather all Israel to Mizpeh, and I will pray for you unto the LORD (1Sa 7:5). The people gathered, and drew water, and poured it out before the LORD, and fasted, and confessed, We have sinned against the LORD; and Samuel judged Israel in Mizpeh (1Sa 7:6). When the Philistines came up against them at that solemn assembly, the LORD thundered upon the enemy and discomfited them, and Samuel took a stone and set it up and called it Ebenezer, saying, Hitherto hath the LORD helped us (1Sa 7:12). The dictionary marks Mizpeh as the watchtower of repentance and prayer. It was on the height of confession, where Israel humbled itself and poured out its heart like water before God, that deliverance came; and the stone of help was raised not over a feat of arms but over a people brought low and lifting up its cry to heaven.
webster_summary: A height of Benjamin where Samuel called Israel to repentance and prayer, and raised the Ebenezer.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that deliverance follows repentance and prayer. It was on the height of Mizpeh, where the people poured out their souls like water and confessed their sin, that the LORD thundered against their enemies and saved them. The Ebenezer was raised not over the strength of Israel but over its weakness humbled before God. So the church learns that her help is found, not in her arms, but in her confession and her cry to heaven.

etymology: Hebrew Nob, perhaps “high place,” a town of the priests near Jerusalem where the tabernacle stood for a time.
biblical_def: Nob was a town of the priests, lying a little north of Jerusalem, where the tabernacle and the priestly house of Ahimelech served in the days of Saul. Thither David fled when he escaped from the court, and Ahimelech the priest, though afraid at his coming, gave him the hallowed shewbread and the sword of Goliath (1Sa 21:1). The Lord Jesus afterward used that very act to teach mercy above ritual, recalling how David entered the house of God and did eat the shewbread, which was not lawful but for the priests (Mat 12:4). But Nob is remembered most for the dreadful vengeance of Saul. When Doeg the Edomite reported what Ahimelech had done, the jealous king commanded the priests slain, and Nob, the city of the priests, he smote with the edge of the sword, both men and women, children and sucklings, and oxen, and asses, and sheep (1Sa 22:19). The dictionary marks Nob as the city of priestly blood, where a king mad with envy turned his sword upon the ministers of God. Centuries later Isaiah set the Assyrian invader at Nob, shaking his hand against the mount of the daughter of Zion (Isa 10:32). The town stands as a witness against the persecution of God’s servants, and a pledge that the blood of His priests is precious in His sight.
webster_summary: A city of the priests near Jerusalem, massacred by Saul after Ahimelech aided David.

corruption_paragraphs: Nob has met no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the scene of one of the bloodiest crimes of Saul’s reign. The dictionary records the town that the reader may know what the envy of a forsaken king did to the priests of the LORD.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the preciousness of the blood of God’s servants and the certain judgment upon their persecutors. Saul, mad with jealousy, smote the city of the priests; Doeg the Edomite did the deed his master commanded. But the blood of the saints is not forgotten in heaven, and the persecutor who lifts his hand against the ministers of God shakes it in vain against the mount of Zion, whose Lord avenges His own.
